subject: Biology
title: Gene Flow: Migration's Genetic Impact
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Gene Flow: Migration's Genetic Impact.

hook.text: When a wolf leaves its pack and joins another, it carries genes that could reshape the new population.

buildup.text: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding.

discovery.text: Gene flow prevents populations from diverging. It keeps distant groups genetically connected.

twist.text: Humans are one of the most genetically uniform species on Earth—because gene flow never stopped.

climax.text: Habitat fragmentation blocks gene flow, isolating populations and accelerating local extinctions.

punchline.text: Migration moves more than bodies. It moves blueprints.

quiz.question: What effect does gene flow have on separate populations?

details.summary: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding. It homogenizes gene pools between connected populations and introduces new genetic variation, counteracting the diversifying effects of natural selection and genetic drift.
details.whyItMatters: Gene flow prevents isolated populations from diverging into separate species and spreads beneficial adaptations across a species' range. It explains why geographically connected populations remain more genetically similar than isolated ones.
takeaways: Even a few migrants per generation can prevent genetic divergence between populations
Gene flow can spread beneficial mutations across a species' range
Barriers to gene flow like mountains and rivers promote speciation

faq.question: How much gene flow is needed to keep populations connected?
faq.answer: Theoretically, just one successful migrant per generation is enough to prevent significant genetic divergence between populations. In practice, more is needed to counteract strong local selection. Even small amounts of gene flow maintain genetic connectivity.

faq.question: Can gene flow be harmful to a population?
faq.answer: Yes. If migrants carry alleles adapted to different environments, gene flow can dilute local adaptations, reducing fitness. This outbreeding depression can be a concern when conservation efforts mix populations from very different habitats.
